## 1 · The dates-as-data tradition, and a persistent puzzle

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
- 40 years of "dates as data" in archaeology (Rick 1987; Williams 2012; Timpson et al. 2014; Crema & Bevan 2021)
- LIRE v3.0 corpus: **180,609 inscriptions** with usable date and findspot (50 BC – AD 350; Kaše et al. 2023, Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.8431452)
- **The recurring objection**: inscription counts reflect *cultural enthusiasm to inscribe* — the **epigraphic habit** — more than anything else (MacMullen 1982; Hanson 2021)
- **Our question**: how much, if any, demographic and structural signal survives once we account properly for editorial distortion in the source data?
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
*Placeholder for opening figure: LIRE temporal coverage at a glance — e.g., 5-year-binned empire SPA with the prominent century-template plateaus visible.*
:::
:::

## 2 · Editorial distortion has a measurable signature

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
*Main figure: the empirical SPA showing the wide-template plateaus and the regnal-cluster spikes. Source: `runs/2026-05-17-empirical-spa-shape/outputs/figures/`.*

Key empirical findings:

- **54.5 %** of `not_before` values end in `01`; **53.0 %** of `not_after` values end in `00`
- The **largest single step in the empirical SPA is at the 1 BC / AD 1 boundary** (+1,159)
- Narrow regnal spikes at AD 77.5 (Flavian), AD 122.5 (Hadrianic), AD 212.5 (Severan)
- **Plateau structure weakens** under narrow-precision filtering; **regnal spikes amplify** (AD 122.5 spike-to-plateau ratio: 1.61× → 13.83×)
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
*Side figure: interval-width distribution showing the bimodal structure (narrow regnal vs wide century templates). Source: `runs/2026-05-17-interval-width-diagnostic/outputs/figures/`.*

**Reading the signature**:

- Wide-template intervals → editorial encoding artefact (mostly modern editor choices)
- Narrow regnal spikes → real ancient clustering (sustained at high-precision)
- BC/AD step → calendar-convention boundary + sparse late-Republic dating
:::
:::

clustering surviving in the precisely-dated subcorpus.

## 3 · What we can resolve: Phase 1 reachability

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
*Main figure: heatmap of detection rate × n across analysis levels for the binding bracket (50 % deviation over ≥ 50 y, Gaussian-tapered). Source: `runs/2026-04-25-h1-simulation/outputs/heatmaps/`.*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Phase 1** asks: at each analysis level, **how many inscriptions does a unit need before our deviation-detection method reliably sees a known effect?**

For the binding 50 %-over-50-y bracket (Gaussian-tapered, conservative):

- **Empire**: reachable at n = 50,000
- **Province**: min n ≈ **1,549** (exp / Gauss; varies 1,385 – 1,938 across nulls)
- **Urban area**: min n ≈ **1,549** for the conservative bracket
- **96 H1-reachable cells** total across empire / province / urban-area subsets

These thresholds **gate** the per-subset deviation-detection analyses for the substantive work.
:::
:::

## 5 · The preregistered fix: Bayesian mixture decomposition

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
**Model** (Decision 19; preregistered):

$$
y_t \sim \mathrm{Multinomial}(N,\ \alpha \cdot p^{\text{conv}}_t + (1-\alpha) \cdot p^{\text{gen}}_t)
$$

- $p^{\text{conv}}$ = empire-wide template-slab structure (century / half-century / reign-interval slabs)
- $p^{\text{gen}}$ = smoothed "real ancient" SPA
- $\alpha$ = empire-level mixing weight

Supplementary fits (Dirichlet-multinomial; rescaled NegBin) reported alongside.

**Validation**: recovery-simulation grid (Decision 21; pinned in design artefact).
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
*[A+ STRETCH] Figure 5 — One synthetic recovery cell. Top: known ground-truth SPA + known α. Bottom: posterior α + recovered genuine SPA. To be generated overnight if time permits; otherwise this slide shows the model schematic + a note that the validation grid is in the prereg.*

**Honest disclosure**:
- Schematic shown; **NOT** the preregistered grid-validated fit
- Full validation runs post-talk
- Preregistration: `osf.io/uycs6` (embargoed)
:::
:::

## 6 · Preliminary scaling: does Hanson population predict inscription count?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
*Main figure: log–log scatter of inscription count vs Hanson 2016 urban population, Rome excluded; frequentist NBR-GLM fit with bootstrap CI band. Source: re-run of notebook cells 197 / 245 with prereg's 50 BC – AD 350 date-window filter.*

**Preliminary frequentist result (date-window-filtered counts; Rome excluded)**:

| Statistic | Value | Comparator |
|---|---|---|
| NBR β (preliminary) | _TBD_ — fit overnight / morning | Hanson 2021: β = **0.672** (95 % CI [0.588, 0.756]) |
| Bootstrap 95 % CI | _TBD_ | Carleton et al. 2025 (elite-honorific): β ≈ 0.3–0.5 |
| n (cities) | _TBD_ ≈ 815 after Rome exclusion | Hanson 2021: 554 sites |
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
**Claim**: population accounts for *some* of the cross-city variation in inscription count — the habit-only critique cannot be the whole story.

**Caveats**:
- Frequentist; preregistered analysis is Bayesian within-between NBR (Mundlak)
- Cumulative (not peak) counts vs Hanson's max-theoretical populations — envelope-vs-envelope
- Hanson populations have their own uncertainty; sensitivity preregistered
- This is **preliminary, post-lodgement**; not a confirmatory test
:::
:::

## Backup slides (not in main 12-min flow)

### B1 · Hanson's residual findings

If asked about replicating Hanson 2021's specific findings:
- Provincial capitals over-produce inscriptions (mean residual 0.43 vs ~0.06 for coloniae / municipia)
- Moran's I = 0.046 on residuals (significant clustering)
- Moran's I = -0.006 on raw counts (no clustering — the clustering is in the residuals)

Our H3c is a preregistered replication of both findings.

### B2 · Why frequentist for the talk?

- The 2024 exploratory pipeline used statsmodels NBR with bootstrap CI
- Re-running it under the prereg-compliant filter takes minutes
- The Bayesian within-between Mundlak NBR is preregistered as the *binding* version
- Frequentist β is a fair preliminary comparator to Hanson 2021's published β = 0.672

### B3 · Why the 50 BC – AD 350 envelope?

- Constrains the data-attribution artefact (late-Republic dating is sparse; post-AD 350 is Late Antique with different epigraphic conventions and different cultural-political context)
- Aligned with Hanson 2016's reference period (100 BC – AD 300, with our extension to AD 350)
- Roughly the imperial-era period during which urban populations and inscription production overlap

### B4 · Why exclude Rome?

- Rome contributes 65,435 inscriptions to the filtered corpus — 36.2 % of the total
- It dominates the scaling fit as a single outlier
- Hanson 2021 also excludes Rome from scaling (Table 7.3 caption)
- Reported transparently; not tested as a sensitivity (per prereg §9)

### B5 · How the mixture model handles year-precise inscriptions

- Year-precise inscriptions ([t, t] encodings; consular or imperial-titulature dating) are *not* part of the convention component
- They remain in the genuine SPA as real ancient anchors
- The convention component is built from the *wide-template* slab structure

### B6 · Hidden Markov model (HMM) post-lodgement extension

If anyone asks about future methodological directions:
- Statistician collaborator (Martin) has proposed a state-space / HMM approach
- Treats latent population N_t as a hidden state under a stationary kernel
- Aoristic-interval emission via Cox-process integration (baorista's existing infrastructure provides the emission layer)
- Genuinely novel for archaeology (no prior art found in our literature scout)
- Would be a post-lodgement OSF amendment if pursued
- Citations: Kéry & Schaub 2012 IPM; Tingley & Huybers 2010 BARCAST
